subject: Biology
title: Superbugs and Antibiotic Resistance
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Superbugs and Antibiotic Resistance.

hook.text: Bacteria are evolving faster than we can make antibiotics. We may be heading to a post-antibiotic era.

buildup.text: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria mutate to survive drugs that once killed them.

discovery.text: MRSA, resistant to multiple drugs, kills more Americans each year than HIV.

twist.text: Overuse of antibiotics in farming—not medicine—drives most global resistance development.

climax.text: Without new strategies, routine surgeries and minor infections could become life-threatening again.

punchline.text: We gave bacteria our best weapons. They adapted.

quiz.question: What drives the most antibiotic resistance globally?

details.summary: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve to survive drugs that once killed them. Overuse of antibiotics in medicine and agriculture accelerates this process, creating superbugs like MRSA that resist multiple drugs and threaten to return medicine to a pre-antibiotic era.
details.whyItMatters: Antibiotic resistance kills over 1.2 million people annually and is projected to cause 10 million deaths per year by 2050 if unchecked. It threatens to make routine surgeries, cancer treatment, and minor infections deadly once again.
takeaways: Bacteria evolve resistance through mutation and horizontal gene transfer
Overuse in medicine and agriculture accelerates resistance development
MRSA and other superbugs resist multiple antibiotic classes simultaneously

faq.question: How do bacteria become resistant to antibiotics?
faq.answer: Random mutations may alter the drug target, produce enzymes that destroy the antibiotic, or create pumps that expel it. Bacteria also share resistance genes horizontally through plasmids. Antibiotic exposure kills susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to multiply unchecked.

faq.question: What can individuals do to slow antibiotic resistance?
faq.answer: Complete prescribed antibiotic courses even when feeling better. Never use antibiotics for viral infections like colds or flu. Avoid demanding antibiotics from doctors when they are not needed. Good hygiene and vaccination reduce infection rates, decreasing antibiotic demand.
